q: What are the best deciduous trees for landscaping?
How do I choose a shade tree for my yard?
What maple tree varieties are best for landscaping?
What is the difference between red oak and white oak?
How do I choose flowering trees like dogwood and redbud?
What are the best small ornamental trees for a front yard?
How do I select trees based on fall color?
What trees grow well in wet soil?
a: Deciduous trees provide seasonal interest with spring flowers, summer shade, fall color, and winter structure. Maple varieties include sugar maple (brilliant orange-red fall color, great for syrup), red maple (adaptable, early red fall color), silver maple (fast-growing but weak wood), and Japanese maple (small, artistic specimen tree). Oak trees are stately and long-lived — red oaks have pointed leaf lobes and fast growth but are less rot-resistant, while white oaks have rounded lobes, slower growth, and exceptional durability. For small spaces, flowering trees like dogwood (spring white or pink flowers), redbud (purple-pink early spring blooms), and cherry (showy spring blossoms) offer spectacular seasonal displays without overwhelming the property.

q: What are the best evergreen trees for landscaping?
How do I choose pine, spruce, and fir trees?
What is the difference between arborvitae and cypress?
How do I use evergreen trees for year-round structure?
What evergreens grow best in shade?
How do I choose a Christmas tree variety for my yard?
What are the most disease-resistant evergreen trees?
How fast do different evergreen trees grow?
a: Evergreen trees provide year-round color, structure, and privacy in the landscape. Pine species include white pine (soft needles, fast-growing), red pine (two-needled clusters, straight trunk), and Austrian pine (dense, dark green, salt-tolerant). Spruce varieties like Colorado Blue Spruce (striking blue needles, pyramidal form) and Norway Spruce (fast-growing, weeping branches) are popular choices. Arborvitae varieties — American (tall native), Emerald Green (narrow, slow-growing), and Green Giant (very fast-growing, 3+ feet per year) — are excellent for hedging. For shade, hemlock (eastern or western) and yew are among the few evergreens that tolerate low light. Leyland cypress grows extremely fast (3-4 feet per year) but is prone to bagworm and canker diseases.

q: What are the best flowering shrubs for landscaping?
How do I choose hydrangea varieties?
What is the difference between bigleaf and panicle hydrangeas?
How do I care for azaleas and rhododendrons?
What are low-maintenance flowering shrubs?
How do I plant a rose garden?
What shrubs bloom all summer?
How do I choose shrubs for fall color?
a: Hydrangeas are among the most popular flowering shrubs, with bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) producing mophead or lacecap blooms in colors affected by soil pH — blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline. Panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata) blooms on new wood with cone-shaped white-to-pink flowers and is more sun-tolerant. Rhododendrons and azaleas thrive in acidic, well-drained soil with dappled shade and are shallow-rooted, requiring consistent moisture. For continuous summer bloom, butterfly bush (Buddleia), spirea, and potentilla flower from early summer through fall. Knock Out roses are disease-resistant, continuous bloomers requiring minimal care, while traditional tea roses need regular deadheading, fertilizing, and disease management.

q: What are evergreen shrubs for foundation planting?
How do I choose boxwood for my garden?
What are the best low-growing evergreen shrubs?
How do I use junipers in landscaping?
What evergreen shrubs grow well in shade?
How do I plant shrubs near my house foundation?
What is the difference between yew and boxwood?
How far from the house should I plant foundation shrubs?
a: Evergreen shrubs provide year-round structure for foundation plantings. Boxwood is the classic choice with varieties from dwarf (Korean boxwood, 2 feet) to tall (American boxwood, 8-10 feet), and thrives in well-drained soil with part shade. Yew (Taxus) is one of the few evergreens that tolerates heavy shade and can be pruned into formal shapes, while Japanese holly offers a boxwood-like appearance with small, glossy leaves. Junipers are sun-loving, drought-tolerant evergreens available in low-growing groundcover forms (Blue Rug) to upright varieties (Hollywood juniper). Plant foundation shrubs at least 3-5 feet from the house to allow for mature growth and air circulation, and avoid covering siding with dense foliage that retains moisture against the building.

What ornamental grasses provide winter interest?
a: Ornamental grasses add texture, movement, and year-round interest to landscapes. Warm-season grasses like miscanthus (maiden grass), pennisetum (fountain grass), and panicum (switchgrass) grow actively in summer and provide fall color and winter structure. Cool-season grasses like calamagrostis (feather reed grass) and festuca (fescue) grow in spring and fall, remaining green during cool weather. Cut back warm-season grasses in late winter or early spring just before new growth appears, leaving them standing through winter for visual interest and wildlife habitat. Fountain grass (Pennisetum alopecuroides) is a versatile, non-invasive choice with fluffy bottlebrush blooms, while Northern sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) tolerates shade and produces distinctive flat seed heads.
